passage: The power cut left the whole lane dark, and the rain drummed on the tin roof. Jahnavi sat cross-legged in front of the small shrine in her room, a single candle lit. Two weeks ago Rafiq, her friend since Class Six, had died. "Why did you take him?" she said aloud. Then louder, her voice cracking: "He was twenty-one! Why?" Nothing answered but rain. She pressed her hand over her mouth, hot with shame. How could she shout at God? In the morning she carried her tea to Ammamma's room and said it all in one breath. Ammamma didn't hurry her. "Beta, He can bear your questions. Ask them. Anger and faith have sat together in many old hearts." Jahnavi let herself cry, and the question stayed.

qa.q: What did Jahnavi do in front of the shrine during the power cut?
qa.a: She sat cross-legged with a single candle lit and asked why Rafiq was taken.

qa.q: Why did Jahnavi feel shame after she shouted?
qa.a: She felt hot with shame because she thought she should not shout at God.

qa.q: What helped Jahnavi after that night?
qa.a: Telling Ammamma everything and being allowed to keep asking her questions rather than being pushed to accept.

qa.q: How might Ammamma see Jahnavi's anger?
qa.a: As something that can sit beside faith, not a betrayal of it, since Ammamma says many old hearts hold both.

grounding: The protagonist, angry with God after a friend's death and ashamed of it, is allowed her questions by a patient elder.

passage:
Dear Charu,

You asked at the prayer meeting why I didn't go inside the temple. I couldn't say it then. I'm angry, Charu. At God. Bhaiya was twenty-six and healthy and good, and one fever took him in four days. Every morning my mother lights the lamp and I stand in the doorway thinking, why him? What was the point?

And then I feel ashamed, because I was raised to trust, and I still half believe.

On Sunday I finally told Pandit ji at our temple. I expected a lecture. He just said, "Ask your questions. Shout them if you need to. Faith that can't hold your anger is too small." He said he'd been angry too, when his son died.

So I'm going back on Thursdays to talk with him. I don't have answers. But I'm not hiding the questions anymore.

Kunal

qa.q: How many days did the fever take Bhaiya?
qa.a: The fever took him in four days.

qa.q: What is Kunal feeling towards God, and what makes it complicated?
qa.a: Kunal feels angry at God, and also ashamed of that anger because Kunal was raised to trust and still half believes.

qa.q: What wise step has Kunal taken with these feelings?
qa.a: Kunal told Pandit ji honestly and will keep meeting him on Thursdays, allowing the questions instead of forcing acceptance.

qa.q: How might Pandit ji see Kunal's anger?
qa.a: Pandit ji seems to see it as part of real faith, not a failure, since he felt it too when his son died.

grounding: The letter shows a young person angry at God after a death and ashamed of it, finding that anger and faith can coexist with a patient guide.

passage:
You asked why I stopped coming to Friday prayers, Reena. It's Rafiq talking, so be patient, I'm not good at this. When Abbu died in March, everyone kept saying, "It was Allah's will, be grateful for the time you had." And I wanted to scream. Grateful? He was fifty-one. He was just about to see me graduate.

I was so angry at Allah that I felt like a traitor. I'd lie on the prayer mat and not say anything.

In June my uncle took me to the old imam at our neighbourhood mosque. I told him everything, even the anger. I thought he'd scold me. He just held my hand and said the prophets also cried and questioned. He said questions are a kind of prayer too.

I still don't have peace. But I go back to him every few weeks. And some Fridays I go to the mosque again.

qa.q: How old was Rafiq's Abbu when he died?
What was Rafiq feeling when people said to be grateful?
qa.a: Rafiq felt furious and wanted to scream, then ashamed, like a traitor to the faith Rafiq grew up in.

qa.q: Which choice helped Rafiq, and why?
qa.a: Talking to the old imam and returning every few weeks helped, because Rafiq could hold anger and faith together instead of forcing acceptance.

qa.q: How might the people who said "be grateful" see the situation differently from Rafiq?
qa.a: They may have meant to comfort Rafiq, but it felt like being told to hide the pain.

grounding: The monologue shows a young person angry at God after a father's death, allowing his questions and finding a patient guide within his faith.
